cells.tense: You are on open ground, and what you build on it is coming up solid.
cells.act: give directions plainly, once, and let them walk
cells.ask: Think of the person still circling that clearing. Give them the route you took through it plainly, in order, once — then stop and leave them to it.
cells.core:
Open ground is where your work goes well. A false thing came down and you didn't stand around mourning it — you started laying the next piece, one solid course at a time, and it's holding. You build best in the clearing, and you don't need the wreckage explained to you first.

The invite is to hand the route over. Pick someone still circling the same clearing, someone who keeps asking what they should do, and give them the directions you found, plainly, once. Say the route in order, from where they stand to where it opens, then stop narrating. Directions that flow don't need enforcing; they land or they don't, and either way your hands are free for the build.
cells.sheetLine: You build best on open ground, and you can hand the route over.
cells.verb: raising the first solid thing on ground something false just vacated
cells.place: the open ground just after a false structure came down

cells.tense: You are bracing for a clearing that hasn't happened yet, and your hands are already rebuilding.
cells.act: walk toward what connects, leaving what does not
cells.ask: Pick a shared thing you've been hollowing out ahead of its time. Walk toward it this week — one unhurried hour inside it, no repair — and let what genuinely connects stay.
cells.core:
You can see the clearing coming before anyone else, and your hands are already rebuilding on ground that hasn't opened. Every shared thing gets examined for what's hollow, and the honest ones come down with the false ones. The people in those things feel it: nothing they're part of stays whole long enough to mean much to them.

What's wanted is contact, not another inspection. Walk toward one shared thing you were about to gut and go deeper into it than is comfortable — sit inside it the way it actually is, unhurried, without fixing. Let what still connects there show itself. That's a different move than clearing. What holds keeps; what doesn't falls once you've stopped pushing it, and you'll have lost nothing you weren't about to lose anyway.
cells.sheetLine: You're tearing shared things down before anyone's finished using them.

cells.tense: You stood at the clearing once, and you are still standing there while the opening closes.
cells.act: make the call and carry it through
cells.ask: Something you decided about this clearing and then left sitting — decide it again, do its first move the same day, and explain nothing to anyone.
cells.core:
The clearing happened. The false thing came down and you were there for it, and then you didn't step onto the ground it opened. You keep meaning to. You know what you'd build. It's all sitting there and no piece of it is getting laid, and the open ground is filling back up with the old arrangement while you wait to feel ready.

What's starved isn't courage; it's a call. Take the smallest piece of what you already decided and act it the same day you decide, in one move, without announcing it to anyone first. No explanation, no checking whether it's allowed. Structure that works moves; it doesn't describe. The step lands on open ground and the ground holds you before you've had time to brace, which is the order that works here.
cells.sheetLine: You know what you'd build. You're waiting to be sure.

cells.tense: The new thing is already half-raised, and you are telling people it built itself.
cells.act: keep the heading when it is contested
cells.ask: The next time someone pushes against what you're building from that clearing, hold your heading — one plain sentence of what you chose, then stay on it without re-arguing the case.
cells.core:
There's something going up out of the clearing, and if anyone asked, you'd say it was the natural next step, what the situation required. It's your work. You made the calls, laid the pieces, held the line when it was contested, and you talk about it like something that happened to you. The people around it take your account as given, so the build stays ground you found.

Go back to when you picked the direction because you wanted it, not because it was assigned. So when the next push comes against what you're building, hold the heading — one plain sentence of what you chose, and stay on it. Saying it once, you'll notice you're defending it. That part you've been leaving off, and it's also the part that's true.
cells.sheetLine: You're defending a heading you say someone else set.
